entries.meaning: A drawn-out open vowel used to stall for a beat while you retrieve a word or soften a hesitant answer. In this hesitation use it is flatter and quieter than the ah of relief or discovery, and Americans reach for it less often than for uh.
examples: I was, ah, hoping we could push the meeting to Thursday.
His name is — ah — it's right on the tip of my tongue.
The total comes to, ah, three hundred and forty dollars.
Ah, how do I say this without sounding rude?
We're, ah, still waiting on legal to sign off.
The witness paused, said ah twice, and then changed his answer.
entries.русский: а-а… / э-э… — протяжный звук раздумья, пока подбираешь слово
entries.variants: ahh, ahhh
entries.see also: uh, um, er, hmm

entries.meaning: The British spelling of the basic hesitation sound, written er because non-rhotic British English pronounces it as a long vowel with no r in it. An American reading the page aloud puts the r back in and says /ɝ/, which is not the sound the spelling was invented for. Americans say uh and write uh; when an American writes er, it is usually in print, in a joking-formal tone, or to mark a small verbal stumble.
examples: The report is due — er — I think it was Friday.
He claims he was at the office all night, which, er, seems unlikely.
So the meeting is at nine, er, nine thirty.
I'd like to introduce our, er, guest of honor.
"Er, I don't think that's quite what she meant," he said.
The transcript is one long string of er and um.
entries.русский: э-э — британское написание звука колебания; американцы говорят и пишут uh
entries.register: regional (chiefly British; in American use mostly a written spelling)
entries.variants: err, uhr
entries.see also: uh, um, erm, ah

entries.meaning: The British counterpart of American um — the same hesitation hum, spelled to match a non-rhotic accent. Americans recognize it in writing but do not normally produce it, and using it out loud in the United States reads as an affectation or as an imitation of a British speaker.
examples: Erm, I'm not sure that's how it works over here.
He wrote back, "Erm, we never actually agreed to that."
The British witness kept saying erm where an American would say um.
Erm — sorry, could you repeat the question?
Her text just said "erm" and nothing else, which was worse than a no.
entries.русский: э-м — брит. аналог американского um
entries.variants: ermm
entries.see also: um, er, uh

entries.meaning: A closed-lip hum meaning that you are thinking, weighing, or not quite convinced. Length carries the meaning: a clipped hm is mild interest or skepticism, while a long hmmm is real deliberation.
examples: Hmm. Let me look at the numbers again before I answer.
"How does eight o'clock work?" "Hmm, could we do eight thirty?"
Hmm, that's strange — the file was here this morning.
She read the offer, said hmm, and slid it back across the table.
Hmmm. I'm not sure I agree with that at all.
He answered every question with a noncommittal hm.
entries.pronunciation note: a hummed m with the lips closed, no vowel in it
entries.русский: хм / хмм — гудение с закрытым ртом: раздумье, сомнение; чем длиннее, тем серьёзнее
entries.variants: hm, hmmm, hmmmm
entries.see also: mm, let me think, well, uh

entries.meaning: A short level hum that fills a pause or signals lukewarm thinking. Note that this is not the pleasure sound mmm (as in mmm, that smells good) and not the agreement sound mm-hmm; the hesitation mm is flat in pitch and goes nowhere.
examples: Mm, I'd have to check my calendar for that week.
"Is the new place any good?" "Mm. It's fine."
He gave a low mm and kept reading.
Mm — maybe. Ask me again after lunch.
"Mm, I'm not sure about the blue one," she said, holding it up to the light.
entries.pronunciation note: a hum on a closed m, no vowel
entries.русский: м-м — ровное мычание, заполняющее паузу; не звук удовольствия и не согласие мм-хмм
entries.variants: mmm
entries.see also: hmm, uh, um

entries.meaning: The default American hesitation sound — a short neutral vowel that holds the floor for the half second it takes to plan the next word. It is normal and near-universal in American speech, and it is edited out of writing entirely except when the writing represents speech.
examples: It's, uh, about a twenty-minute drive from here.
Uh, I think you may have the wrong number.
We're looking at, uh, maybe three or four candidates.
"What's the password?" "Uh … hang on, I wrote it down somewhere."
He said uh eleven times in a two-minute answer.
I was going to — uh — sorry, what was the question again?
entries.русский: э-э — основной американский звук колебания; только в устной речи
entries.variants: uhh, uhhh, er (British spelling)
entries.see also: um, er, ah, hmm, like

entries.meaning: The other core American filler: a hum that ends with the lips closing, used like uh but typically before a longer or more delicate stretch of speech. It often carries a note of awkwardness, and a written um in a text message almost always means "I have a problem with what you just said."
examples: The deadline is, um, next Tuesday, I think.
Um, is this seat taken?
Um, you do know she's his sister, right?
She started every answer with um and then finished it confidently.
Can I, um, ask you something kind of personal?
He texted back a single "um" and I knew I had messed up.
entries.русский: э-м / м-м — второй основной филлер, часто с оттенком неловкости
entries.variants: umm, ummm, erm (British spelling)
entries.see also: uh, erm, hmm, well, like

entries.meaning: Takes the floor back after an interruption and signals that you are picking up the exact thread you were on. Said mildly it is just bookkeeping; said flatly to the person who cut you off, it is a rebuke with no rude word in it.
examples: As I was saying, the permits won't clear until March.
Sorry, the dog got out — as I was saying, we'd need two more people to pull this off.
Like I was saying, nobody on that call had actually read the contract.
He waited for the laughter to die down. "As I was saying …"
As I was saying before the fire drill, there are three options on the table.
entries.русский: как я уже говорил — возврат к прерванной мысли; может звучать как упрёк перебившему
entries.register: neutral (can sound pointed after an interruption)
entries.variants: like I was saying, as I said, anyway, as I was saying
entries.see also: where was I, anyway, so anyway, hold on

entries.meaning: A request for the listener's patience while you find a file, work something out, or talk your way through a half-formed idea. It is polite enough for a client call and casual enough for a friend.
examples: Bear with me — I know that invoice is in here somewhere.
Bear with me a second while I pull up the slides.
This is going to sound crazy, so bear with me.
"Bear with me, folks, we're having a technical issue."
Bear with me here, the math takes a minute to explain.
entries.русский: потерпите немного / подождите чуть-чуть — просьба дать время разобраться
entries.variants: bear with me a second, bear with me here
entries.see also: hold on, just a second, hang on, hear me out

entries.meaning: A casual "stop and wait" — used to buy yourself a moment, to interrupt someone mid-flow, or to flag that something they just said does not add up.
examples: Hang on, let me grab a pen.
Hang on a sec — I think that's my phone.
Hang on, you said the store closes at six?
"Ready to go?" "Hang on, I'm still tying my shoes."
Hang on, I know exactly who you mean now.
entries.русский: погоди / секунду — разг. «стой и подожди»
entries.variants: hang on a sec, hang on a minute
entries.see also: hold on, wait, just a second, bear with me

entries.meaning: Asks the listener to hold their objection until you have finished, and admits up front that the idea is going to sound bad at first. It is a floor-holding move rather than a stall: it buys the whole rest of your turn instead of a single beat.
examples: Hear me out — what if we drove instead of flying?
I know how this sounds, but hear me out.
"Absolutely not." "Just hear me out for thirty seconds."
Hear me out on this: we cancel the party and take the money to the beach.
He held up a hand and said, "Hear me out before you say no."
entries.русский: выслушай меня до конца — не перебивай, пока не договорю
entries.variants: just hear me out, hear me out on this
entries.see also: bear with me, hold on, look, listen

entries.meaning: A request to pause. It works both as a stall while you look something up and as a mild objection that stops the other person so you can catch up.
examples: Hold on, I'll transfer you to someone who can help with that.
Hold on — did you just say she quit?
Hold on a second, I want to write this down.
"Hold on, I've got another call coming in."
Hold up, that's not what the email said at all.
entries.русский: подождите / постойте — просьба сделать паузу либо мягкое возражение
entries.variants: hold on a second, hold up, hold on there
entries.see also: hang on, wait, just a second, bear with me

entries.meaning: A stall announcing that you are choosing your words because what comes next is awkward, critical, or delicate. It warns the listener that a blunt opinion or some bad news is on the way.
examples: How do I put this — you're not really a morning person, are you?
The apartment is, how do I put this, cozy.
How should I put this? He's not the strongest writer on the team.
She's, how do I say this, very direct with clients.
How do I put this delicately? Your car is not worth fixing.
entries.русский: как бы это сказать — подбираю слова перед чем-то неловким или неприятным
entries.variants: how should I put this, how do I say this, how do I put it
entries.see also: what's the word, let me think, I mean, well

entries.meaning: A short promise that the pause will be brief, used when you have to finish something before you can answer or move on.
examples: Just a second — I'm almost done with this email.
"Can you come here?" "One sec!"
Just a sec, let me put you on speaker.
Give me a second to think about how to answer that.
One second and I'll have the total for you.
entries.русский: секундочку / минутку — обещание, что пауза будет короткой
entries.variants: just a sec, one sec, one second, give me a second, gimme a sec
entries.see also: hold on, hang on, bear with me, let's see

entries.meaning: An explicit announcement that you are working out an answer rather than dodging the question. Said briskly it simply buys time; said slowly, it often signals that the answer is going to be no.
examples: Let me think — I want to say it was 2019?
"What's the fastest route from here?" "Let me think for a second."
Let me think about it and I'll get back to you tomorrow.
Let me think. There were four of us at dinner, maybe five.
Hmm, let me think how to explain this without the jargon.
entries.русский: дай(те) подумать — я обдумываю ответ, а не увиливаю
entries.variants: let me think for a second, let me think about it
entries.see also: let's see, hmm, hold on, that's a good question, where was I

entries.meaning: A stall used while you scan, count, or search — the verbal equivalent of running a finger down a list. It is the standard thing Americans say out loud while looking something up.
examples: Let's see — I've got Tuesday at ten or Thursday at two.
Let me see, where on earth did I park?
"How many people are coming?" "Let's see … eleven, counting the kids."
Let's see here, your account was opened back in March.
So we need milk, bread, and, let's see, coffee.
entries.русский: так, посмотрим / сейчас — пока ищешь, считаешь или просматриваешь список
entries.variants: let me see, let's see here, let's see now
entries.see also: let me think, hmm, what's the word, just a second

entries.meaning: Buys several seconds while you assemble an answer, and flatters the asker on the way in. Everyone recognizes what it is doing, which is why it carries a faint smell of the press conference and the job interview — and why a bare good question sometimes means "I have no idea."
examples: "How much would that cost us?" "That's a good question — let me run the numbers."
Good question. I honestly don't know.
She asked why the policy exists at all, and all I had was "that's a good question."
"Why is it spelled that way?" "That's a great question, and the answer is that nobody knows."
That's a fair question, and I'd rather answer it once I've seen the report.
entries.русский: хороший вопрос — тянет время и льстит спросившему; часто значит «понятия не имею»
entries.variants: good question, that's a great question, that's a fair question
entries.see also: let me think, let's see, how do I put this, bear with me

entries.meaning: A one-word brake on the conversation that stalls the other speaker while you catch up. In American speech it very often introduces a realization or a correction — wait rarely means "wait quietly," it means "something just registered."
examples: Wait — I think I left my keys in the car.
Wait a second, weren't you supposed to be in Denver today?
"It's the third one on the left." "Wait, coming from which direction?"
Wait wait wait, start over from the part about the dog.
Wait, so you two already knew each other?
entries.русский: стой / погоди — резкая остановка разговора, обычно перед «до меня дошло»
entries.register: informal (blunt when it cuts someone off mid-sentence)
entries.variants: wait a second, wait a minute, wait wait wait
entries.see also: hold on, hang on, hmm, actually

entries.meaning: The standard American way to flag that you are hunting for a specific word and would welcome help finding it. It is usually dropped into the middle of a sentence, which then resumes once the word arrives.
examples: It's one of those — what's the word — collapsible chairs.
He was being deliberately, what's the word, evasive.
What do you call it, the thing that holds the door open?
She had a look of, what's the word, resignation.
It's a kind of pasta, what's it called, orecchiette.
entries.русский: как это называется / как бы сказать — ищу нужное слово и жду подсказки
entries.variants: what's the word for it, what do you call it, what's it called
entries.see also: whatchamacallit, thingy, whatsit, how do I put this

entries.meaning: Said after an interruption to find your place again in your own story or explanation. It quietly asks the listener to hand the thread back to you.
examples: Sorry — where was I? Oh, right, the flight.
Now where was I? Ah yes, the third-quarter numbers.
"Where were we?" "You were telling us about your neighbor."
Give me a second, I lost my train of thought. Where was I?
Okay, where was I — the part where the car wouldn't start.
entries.русский: на чём я остановился — попытка найти нить после того, как перебили
entries.variants: where were we, now where was I
entries.see also: as I was saying, anyway, so anyway, let me think

entries.meaning: Flags that what follows corrects, contradicts, or gently surprises — either fixing what was just said or introducing a fact the listener would not expect. At the front of a sentence it can sound corrective, so Americans often cushion it with well or a smile.
examples: Actually, the meeting got moved to Thursday.
"You've never been to Chicago, right?" "Actually, I lived there for two years."
I thought it would be a nightmare, but it was actually pretty easy.
Actually, on second thought, I'll have the salmon.
That's not a bad idea, actually.
entries.русский: на самом деле / вообще-то — поправка или неожиданный для собеседника факт
entries.see also: I mean, well, right, basically, technically

entries.meaning: A resetting marker that closes off what came before and starts the next thing — the sound of a teacher beginning class or a driver putting the car in gear. With rising pitch at the end of a sentence it becomes a check: alright? means "are we good so far?"
examples: Alright, let's get started.
Alright, so the first thing you'll need is a screwdriver.
"Alright, everybody up — we're leaving in ten minutes."
We'll meet at the north entrance at six, alright?
Alright, I'll let you go — say hi to your mom for me.
entries.русский: ладно / так — закрывает предыдущее и открывает следующее; в конце фразы — «договорились?»
entries.register: informal (the two-word spelling all right is the one for formal prose)
entries.variants: all right, aight, a'ight
entries.see also: okay, right, so, now

entries.meaning: An older, folksier twin of anyway, used to drop a digression and get back to the point or to wrap a story up. Younger speakers use it far less often than anyway.
examples: Anyhow, that's how we ended up with three cats.
It rained all weekend. Anyhow, how was your trip?
I don't know what he was thinking. Anyhow, it's done now.
Anyhow, I should let you go.
She never did call back. Anyhow, no harm done.
entries.русский: в общем / так или иначе — разг., слегка устаревший вариант anyway
entries.register: informal (slightly dated; most common in the South and Midwest)
entries.variants: anyhoo, anywho, any old how
entries.see also: anyway, so anyway, well

entries.meaning: The workhorse of topic management: it ends a digression and returns to the main thread, or signals that you are winding the conversation down. Left hanging at the end of a turn, it means roughly "so that's that."
examples: Anyway, back to what I was saying about the budget.
Anyway, it's getting late — I should head out.
The food was mediocre and the service was slow. Anyway.
Anyways, we ended up driving instead of flying.
He may never forgive me. Anyway, I did what I had to do.
entries.русский: в общем / ладно — возврат к теме после отступления или сворачивание разговора
entries.register: neutral (anyways is very informal and widely treated as nonstandard)
entries.variants: anyways
entries.see also: anyhow, so anyway, well, where was I

entries.meaning: Announces a simplified version — the short answer, with the details filed off. In casual speech it has drifted into a near-filler that adds little beyond "here comes my summary."
examples: Basically, the engine needs to be replaced.
"How does the refund work?" "Basically, you have thirty days to change your mind."
Basically what happened is she got a better offer.
We spent basically the whole weekend cleaning.
He's basically running the department at this point.
entries.русский: по сути / в общем — дальше короткая версия без подробностей
entries.register: neutral in its "here is the short version" sense; informal as a filler
entries.see also: I mean, kind of, pretty much, literally, so

entries.meaning: Introduces a side remark that is not part of the current topic, often a small piece of news the speaker does not want to make a production of. The written abbreviation BTW is standard in email and texts.
examples: By the way, your package came while you were out.
I ran into Marcus yesterday — by the way, he says hi.
By the way, do you still have my ladder?
The rent is going up in January, by the way.
BTW, I moved our call to three.
entries.русский: кстати / между прочим — попутное замечание не по текущей теме
entries.register: neutral (the abbreviation BTW is informal, for email and texts only)
entries.variants: BTW, btw, by the by
entries.see also: speaking of which, that reminds me, anyway, now, come to think of it

entries.meaning: Marks something that has surfaced in your head while you were saying something else — usually a detail that quietly changes the picture. Unlike that reminds me, what surfaces is still attached to the point at hand instead of opening a new topic.
examples: Come to think of it, I haven't seen him since the wedding.
She never did answer that email, come to think of it.
Come to think of it, the car was making that same noise last week.
"Was anyone else in the building?" "Now that I think about it, the cleaning crew was still there."
You two would probably get along, come to think of it.
entries.русский: если подумать / а ведь правда — деталь, всплывшая в голове прямо сейчас
entries.variants: now that I think about it, come to think about it, thinking about it
entries.see also: that reminds me, speaking of which, by the way, actually

entries.meaning: Hands the other side one point before you argue against it, so that the rest of your position looks even-handed. It is nearly always followed, sooner or later, by a but, and standing alone as a full turn it is a grudging half-concession.
examples: Granted, the first hour is slow, but it's worth staying for the ending.
He's the youngest person on the staff, granted, and he still outworks everyone.
Granted, I only heard one side of it.
"It's cheaper to fly out of the other airport." "Granted. It's also two hours away."
Granted, we've blown a deadline before — that's exactly why I'm asking now.
entries.русский: допустим / надо признать — уступка перед возражением; дальше почти всегда «но»
entries.variants: granted, though, admittedly, I'll grant you that
entries.see also: that said, to be fair, actually, well

entries.meaning: Announces the complication — the fact that explains why the obvious answer will not work. It promises the listener the real story, which makes it a favorite of people who are about to deliver bad news gently.
examples: Here's the thing: we already paid for the tickets.
I'd love to help, but here's the thing — I'm out of town all week.
The thing is, nobody ever asked the customers.
"Just call and cancel." "Here's the thing, the deposit isn't refundable."
Here's the thing though — she was right about the timeline.
entries.русский: дело вот в чём — сейчас будет то самое осложнение
entries.variants: the thing is, here's the thing though, the thing about it is
entries.see also: look, see, I mean, that said, well

entries.meaning: Restates what was just said in plainer or blunter terms, either to make it clearer or to drag the real meaning into the open. It is the neutral, printable cousin of I mean — and turned flatly on someone else's explanation, it becomes an accusation.
examples: In other words, we're starting over.
The lease runs through August — in other words, you have four more months.
"The role is being restructured." "In other words, I'm fired?"
Put another way, every dollar we save here costs us two next year.
She wants the schedule and the budget; in other words, the whole project.
entries.русский: другими словами / иначе говоря — пересказ сказанного проще или прямее
entries.register: neutral (at home in writing as well as speech)
entries.variants: or rather, put another way, which is to say
entries.see also: I mean, basically, so to speak, that said

entries.meaning: Demands the listener's full attention before something important, blunt, or final. It carries more edge than look, so tone does the work: a warm listen is confiding, a flat one is a warning.
examples: Listen, I'm not going to pretend this is easy.
Listen, you've got nothing to apologize for.
"Listen up, everybody — buses leave at eight sharp."
Listen, if you don't want to go, just say so.
Now listen, I've told you three times already.
entries.русский: послушай(те) — требование внимания перед чем-то важным или резким
entries.variants: listen up, now listen
entries.see also: look, see, okay

entries.meaning: Announces that you are skipping the middle of a story and going straight to how it came out. Speakers often reach for it only after they have already talked for five minutes, which is half the joke of it.
examples: Long story short, we missed the flight and drove all night.
He talked for ten minutes and then said, "Long story short, we're out of money."
To make a long story short, the roof is fine and the basement isn't.
"How'd the meeting go?" "Long story short, they want a redesign."
Long story short: don't lend him your car.
entries.русский: короче говоря / если вкратце — пропускаю середину истории
entries.variants: to make a long story short, long story, to cut a long story short (chiefly British)
entries.see also: anyway, so anyway, basically, yada yada

entries.meaning: Marks that you are cutting through the back-and-forth to state your real position. Politicians and managers lean on it constantly; used too often, it reads as impatience.
examples: Look, we've all made mistakes.
Look, the numbers just don't support it.
"Look, I'll be honest with you — we can't match that price."
Look, can we talk about this after dinner?
Now look, nobody is blaming you.
entries.русский: слушай / смотри — перехожу к сути, к своей настоящей позиции
entries.variants: now look, look here (dated)
entries.see also: listen, see, here's the thing, I mean, well

entries.meaning: Moves the conversation on to the next step or the next item, with no reference to time at all. It also softens a coming correction, as in Now, that's not quite what I said.
examples: Now, where would you like to start?
We've covered the budget. Now, about the schedule.
Now, I'm not saying she was wrong.
Now then, who wants dessert?
Add the eggs one at a time. Now, slowly fold in the flour.
entries.русский: так / итак — переход к следующему пункту, без значения времени
entries.variants: now then, and now
entries.see also: so, then, okay, alright

entries.meaning: The all-purpose transition: it closes the previous topic and opens the next one, and with rising pitch it checks that the listener is still with you. Note that a drawn-out okaaay signals doubt, not agreement.
examples: Okay, let's take it from the top.
Okay, so what you want to do is press and hold the button.
Turn left at the light, okay? Then it's the second driveway.
"Okay, everyone, eyes up here."
Okay … that's not what I expected to hear.
'Kay, see you at six.
entries.русский: ладно / так / ну хорошо — универсальный переход; с вопросительной интонацией — «ясно?»
entries.variants: OK, O.K., 'kay, mkay, okey-dokey
entries.see also: alright, so, right, now

entries.meaning: Two jobs. (1) As an opener it marks a fresh start or a return to business. (2) Tacked onto the end of a clause with rising pitch, it checks that the listener agrees or is still following — though repeated right? tags can sound pushy in an argument.
examples: Right, let's figure out who's driving.
So we're meeting at the office first, right?
You've done this before, right?
Right — first question: who's the audience?
It was raining, right, and none of us had an umbrella.
"The blue one?" "Right."
entries.русский: так / итак — начало нового этапа; в конце фразы с вопросом — «верно?, да?»
entries.variants: right?, right then, all right
entries.see also: okay, alright, you know, so

entries.meaning: Introduces the explanation the listener has been waiting for, often a little defensively — see frames what follows as the reason things are the way they are.
examples: See, the problem is that nobody told the client.
I would have called, y'see, but my phone was dead.
See, that's exactly what I was afraid of.
It's not that I don't want to go. See, I already promised my sister.
See, this is why we keep a spare key under the mat.
entries.русский: понимаешь / видишь ли — разг., вводит объяснение, часто чуть оправдываясь
entries.variants: see, the thing is, y'see
entries.see also: you see, look, I mean, listen

entries.meaning: The most common way Americans open a turn: it introduces a topic, launches a question, or draws a conclusion from what came before. A stretched sooo at the start of a sentence usually means awkward news is coming.
examples: So, how did the interview go?
So I'm standing in line at the bank, and my phone rings.
The store closes at six, so — we should probably head out.
Sooo, slight change of plans.
So, to summarize: we need two more weeks and one more engineer.
"So? What did she say?"
entries.русский: итак / так вот / ну — самый частый способ начать реплику или подвести итог
entries.variants: sooo
entries.see also: so anyway, well, okay, anyway

entries.meaning: A doubled marker used to abandon a side story and get back on track — the so pushes forward while the anyway dismisses the digression, which is exactly what a rambling storyteller needs.
examples: So anyway, we finally got the car started around midnight.
So anyway, that's why I don't eat at that place anymore.
So anyways, she calls me the next morning like nothing happened.
Long story. So anyway, how's your mom doing?
So anyway, where do you want to eat tonight?
entries.русский: ну так вот / в общем — бросаю отступление и возвращаюсь к главному
entries.variants: so anyways, anyway so
entries.see also: anyway, so, anyhow, where was I

entries.meaning: Closes out a turn that has run out of steam: the point has been made, there is no tidy ending available, and so yeah hands the floor back. It is the spoken equivalent of a shrug at the end of a paragraph, and it is everywhere in the speech of Americans under about forty.
examples: It's a long commute, but the pay is better. So yeah.
We tried it, it didn't work, so yeah — back to the drawing board.
That's pretty much the whole plan, so yeah, let me know what you think.
She hasn't called me since. So yeah, I'd say we're done.
So yeah — that was my Tuesday.
entries.русский: ну вот, как-то так — очень разг., закрывает выдохшуюся реплику
entries.variants: so yeah, anyway, and yeah, so, yeah
entries.see also: anyway, so, you know, I guess

entries.meaning: Hooks a new topic onto the one just mentioned, so that changing the subject looks like a natural step instead of an interruption. Americans use it to raise something they have been waiting all conversation for an opening to bring up.
examples: Speaking of which, did you ever hear back about the apartment?
We're driving up Friday. Speaking of which, do you still need a ride?
"Traffic was awful this morning." "Speaking of, I think your registration expired."
Speaking of which, I still owe you twenty dollars.
The budget's due Monday — speaking of which, I need your numbers by Thursday.
entries.русский: кстати о / раз уж зашла речь — цепляет новую тему за только что сказанное
entries.variants: speaking of, speaking of that, which reminds me
entries.see also: that reminds me, by the way, anyway, now

entries.meaning: Credits the other person's remark with knocking loose a subject of your own. Like speaking of which it softens a change of topic, but it points at something you had genuinely forgotten until that second.
examples: That reminds me — your mother called while you were out.
Oh, that reminds me, I need to renew my passport before June.
"The Hendersons are moving." "That reminds me, we never sent them a card."
He mentioned the storm, which reminds me — is your power back on?
That reminds me, we're almost out of coffee filters.
entries.русский: кстати, вспомнил / это мне напомнило — тема, всплывшая от слов собеседника
entries.variants: which reminds me, oh, that reminds me, before I forget
entries.see also: speaking of which, by the way, anyway, now

entries.meaning: Concedes the point you have just made and then pushes back against it. It is the courteous way to say but, and unlike most of this file it is at home in writing as well as speech.
examples: The price is high. That said, you're not going to find another one like it.
I'm not thrilled about the hours. That being said, I'd take the job.
She's new here. That said, she should have caught this.
It rained the entire week — that said, we'd go back tomorrow.
Having said that, nobody is forcing you to sign anything today.
entries.русский: при этом / тем не менее / и всё же — вежливое «но» после уступки
entries.variants: that being said, having said that, all that said
entries.see also: granted, actually, anyway, well, I mean

entries.meaning: Tacked onto the end of a clause, it draws a conclusion from what has just been established: "given all that." At the front, paired with well or okay, it closes a decision out.
examples: You're all set, then.
"I can't make Friday." "Monday it is, then."
Well then, I guess we're driving.
So it isn't broken, then?
Okay then, let's call it a night.
entries.русский: тогда / значит — в конце фразы делает вывод из сказанного
entries.variants: well then, okay then, right then
entries.see also: so, now, okay, well, alright

entries.meaning: The classic hesitation opener. It buys a beat before an answer and warns that the answer will not be a simple yes — a reservation, a qualification, or some bad news is coming. Stretched out, welllll is almost a polite no all by itself.
examples: Well, that's one way to look at it.
"Did you like it?" "Well … it wasn't really my thing."
Well, I suppose we could try again next month.
Well, look who finally showed up.
Well, to be honest, I'd rather stay home.
Welll, technically the deadline was yesterday.
entries.русский: ну / что ж — классическая пауза перед ответом, который не будет простым «да»
entries.variants: welll, well now, well then
entries.see also: um, so, actually, hmm, I mean

entries.meaning: A distinctly American pair in which the first word acknowledges what you just said and the second delivers the actual answer: yeah no means "I hear you, but no," and no yeah means "I hear your doubt, but yes." Speakers are usually unaware they are doing it.
examples: "Want to come to the thing on Saturday?" "Yeah no, I'm gonna pass."
No yeah, it's a great movie — you should definitely see it.
Yeah no, I hear you, but the schedule isn't moving.
Yeah no for sure, I'll send it over tonight.
"You didn't hate it?" "No yeah, I actually liked it a lot."
entries.русский: да нет / нет да — разг.: первое слово признаёт сказанное, второе даёт настоящий ответ
entries.variants: no yeah, yeah no for sure, nah yeah
entries.see also: right, okay, I mean, well

entries.meaning: Announces a decision or an opinion the speaker has arrived at just this second, usually with a change of direction behind it. Despite the shared words it is not the filler you know — it is a small drumroll, and what follows is the whole point of the sentence.
examples: You know what? Let's just take my car.
You know what, forget I said anything.
You know what — I think she was right the whole time.
"We could push it to next week." "You know what? That would help a lot."
You know what, I'm going to bed.
entries.русский: знаешь что — объявляет решение или мнение, возникшее прямо сейчас
entries.variants: y'know what, you know what, never mind, tell you what
entries.see also: you know, actually, okay, alright

entries.meaning: Marks the explanation of something the listener did not know, presenting it as the key that makes everything make sense. Overused it turns into lecturing, which is why it is so common in teaching and in period fiction.
examples: The bridge was out, you see, so we had to go the long way around.
You see, the two accounts were never actually linked.
He'd already sold the house, you see. Nobody had told her.
Ya see, that's where most people get it wrong.
It isn't the cost, you see — it's the timing.
entries.русский: видишь ли / понимаете ли — вводит объяснение; может звучать назидательно
entries.variants: ya see, don't you see
entries.see also: see, look, I mean, listen

entries.meaning: Closes a list on the understanding that the pattern keeps going. It is the plain, printable version of and stuff and and whatnot; doubling it into and so on and so forth usually signals impatience with the list rather than a longer one.
examples: Bring a sleeping bag, a flashlight, bug spray, and so on.
The form wants your address, your previous address, and so forth.
We went through the whole routine — deep breaths, count to ten, and so on.
He had an excuse for everything: traffic, the weather, his alarm, and so on and so forth.
It's the usual argument about who pays and who drives and so on.
entries.русский: и так далее / и тому подобное — закрывает список; единственный в группе уместен на письме
entries.register: neutral (the one list-closer in this group that survives in writing)
entries.variants: and so forth, and so on and so forth, etc.
entries.see also: and stuff, and whatnot, or whatever, yada yada, blah blah blah

entries.meaning: A tag that closes a list without finishing it, implying more of the same. It is casual to the point of sloppiness — fine with friends, weak in a job interview.
examples: We just hung out, watched a movie and stuff.
She's into hiking and camping and all that.
I have to do laundry and stuff before we leave.
They gave us pens and notebooks and stuff like that.
He was talking about interest rates and stuff — I tuned out.
entries.русский: и всё такое — очень разг., обрывает список на середине
entries.variants: and stuff like that, and all that, and everything, and all
entries.see also: or something, or whatever, and whatnot, and so on, like, you know

entries.meaning: Closes an unfinished list the way and stuff does, but with a faintly old-fashioned flavor. It is common in the speech of older Americans, in the trades, and anywhere a list is too tedious to finish.
examples: She brought paper plates, napkins, and whatnot.
We spent the whole morning filling out forms and whatnot.
He does drywall, tile, and whatnot — whatever the job needs.
There's a box of cables and what have you out in the garage.
They talked about the weather, the neighbors, and whatnot, for a solid hour before anyone brought up the money.
entries.русский: и всякое такое / и прочее — разг., слегка старомодно-простецки
entries.register: informal (folksy; reads as older or small-town)
entries.variants: and what have you, and such, and whatnot else
entries.see also: and stuff, and so on, or whatever, or something, yada yada

entries.meaning: The reduced spoken form of "I don't know," used less as a real admission of ignorance than as a hedge that softens an opinion you are about to give anyway. Written out, it deliberately marks casual speech.
examples: I dunno, it just doesn't feel right to me.
"Where should we eat?" "I dunno, you pick."
I dunno, maybe he was just having a bad day.
It's, I dunno, forty minutes north of the city?
"Dunno," she said, without looking up.
entries.русский: да не знаю / ну не знаю — очень разг., чаще смягчает мнение, чем признаёт незнание
entries.variants: dunno, iunno, I donno
entries.see also: I guess, I feel like, kind of, or something

entries.meaning: Frames an opinion as a personal impression rather than a claim about the world, which makes it harder to argue with and easier to walk back. In casual American speech it has largely taken over the ground that I think used to hold.
examples: I feel like we've had this exact conversation before.
I feel like she wasn't really listening to a word of it.
Honestly, I feel like the first draft was better.
"Should we wait for him?" "I feel like we should just go."
I feel like nobody actually reads these emails.
entries.русский: мне кажется / у меня ощущение, что — подаёт мнение как личное впечатление
entries.variants: I feel like maybe, I kind of feel like
entries.see also: I guess, I mean, kind of, to be honest

entries.meaning: Marks reluctant or low-confidence agreement — you accept the conclusion without any enthusiasm for it. At the end of a sentence it drains the certainty out of whatever came before.
examples: I guess we could leave a little earlier.
"Is that everything?" "I guess so."
It's fine, I guess. I just expected more.
I guess I should have read the fine print.
She's the most qualified, I guess, but I'd still interview the others.
entries.русский: наверное / пожалуй — неохотное согласие без всякого энтузиазма
entries.variants: I guess so, guess so, I suppose
entries.see also: I dunno, I feel like, I want to say, kind of, sort of

entries.meaning: Repairs, restates, or braces what you just said: you are rewording for accuracy, or you are about to defend an opinion. In fast speech it has also become a plain turn-opening filler with no repair work to do.
examples: It's expensive — I mean, not outrageous, but more than I wanted to spend.
I mean, what was he supposed to do?
She's my cousin. I mean, technically my second cousin.
I mean, I'd help, but I'll be out of town that week.
He was upset. I mean, he was really upset.
entries.русский: то есть / я имею в виду — поправка или уточнение; в быстрой речи просто филлер
entries.variants: I mean like
entries.see also: like, you know, actually, well, see, in other words

entries.respell: eye WAHNT tuh say, casually eye WAH-nuh say
entries.meaning: Introduces a half-remembered fact — a year, a price, a name — and marks it as the speaker's best guess rather than a claim. It is usually delivered with rising, question-like intonation, and it openly invites correction.
examples: I want to say it was 2015, but don't quote me.
"How far is it?" "I want to say forty miles?"
Her sister's name is — I wanna say Diane?
I want to say there were about a dozen of us at that dinner.
Rent was, I want to say, eleven hundred a month back then.
entries.русский: кажется / вроде бы — вводит полузабытый факт как догадку, с готовностью к поправке
entries.variants: I wanna say, I want to say something like
entries.see also: I guess, I dunno, or so, let me think, -ish

entries.meaning: A closing hedge that admits your explanation may have come out muddled and invites the listener to say so. It is polite self-deprecation rather than a real question.
examples: It's more of a feeling than an argument, if that makes sense.
I want something structured but not rigid, if that makes sense.
She's not unfriendly, just very private — if that makes any sense.
We're rebuilding it while it's still running, if that makes sense.
So it's a hobby that pays for itself, if that makes sense.
entries.русский: если понятно, о чём я — признаёт, что объяснение вышло, может быть, путаным
entries.variants: if that makes any sense, does that make sense
entries.see also: you know, I mean, kind of, sort of

entries.meaning: A suffix that has broken loose and become a standalone hedge meaning "approximately" or "not exactly." As a one-word answer it softens a time, a number, or a lukewarm yes.
examples: "Are you free around seven?" "Ish. Make it seven fifteen."
Dinner's at eight, ish — don't stress about the traffic.
There were fifty people there, ish.
The house is Victorian, ish — somebody tacked a wing on it in the seventies.
"Is the draft done?" "Ish. I still have to proofread it."
entries.русский: примерно / вроде того — суффикс, оторвавшийся в самостоятельное «приблизительно»
entries.see also: kind of, sort of, or so, I guess

entries.meaning: Softens a claim to "somewhat" or "not entirely," lowering the temperature of an adjective, a verb, or a whole statement. It is one of the most common American hedges and is unmistakably casual on the page.
examples: I kind of wanted to stay home tonight.
It's kinda cold in here — do you mind if I close the window?
"Do you like it?" "Kind of. Not as much as the first one."
He kind of implied that the job was already mine.
That's kinda the whole point.
entries.русский: вроде / как бы / отчасти — разг., смягчает утверждение до «в некоторой степени»
entries.variants: kinda, kind of like
entries.see also: sort of, -ish, pretty much, like, I guess

entries.meaning: Three filler jobs, all separate from the verb like. (1) A hesitation marker that holds the floor. (2) An approximator meaning "about." (3) A quotative with be, introducing speech or thought, as in he was like, "no way." All three are extremely common in American speech and all three are out of place in formal settings.
examples: It was, like, the best day of the whole trip.
There were like forty people crammed into that apartment.
And she was like, "You're seriously not coming?"
It's not far — like, twenty minutes?
He just, like, walked out in the middle of the meeting.
I'm like ninety percent sure I locked the door.
entries.русский: типа / как бы — филлер; также «примерно» перед числом и ввод речи: «он такой: ни за что»
entries.see also: you know, I mean, um, or something, kind of

entries.meaning: Once strictly "in the exact sense," now used mostly as an intensifier for something figurative, and in the loosest speech as a near-empty emphasis filler. The intensifier use is ordinary in casual American speech and still draws complaints in formal writing.
examples: I literally just walked in the door — let me call you back.
My phone literally died in the middle of the call.
There were literally a thousand emails waiting for me.
She literally cannot say no to anyone.
We showed up literally wearing the same jacket.
He took the instructions literally and painted the whole wall. (the original sense)
entries.русский: буквально — изначально «в прямом смысле», теперь чаще усилитель «реально, прямо»
entries.register: informal as an intensifier; neutral in its original "to the letter" sense
entries.see also: basically, actually, like, so to speak, technically

entries.meaning: Marks a statement as true in the main but not in every detail — "approximately," "in effect." It hedges numbers, descriptions, and whole conclusions, and unlike most of this file it is respectable enough for a written report.
examples: The job is done, more or less.
We agreed on the terms, more or less.
It's more or less the same recipe my grandmother used.
"Is that everyone?" "More or less — two people are calling in."
He runs the place, more or less, whatever his title says.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle word reduces to a plain r-colored vowel
entries.русский: более или менее / в общем и целом — верно в главном, но не в каждой детали
entries.see also: pretty much, kind of, sort of, or so

entries.meaning: Follows a number, a time, or a distance to mark it as an estimate. It is tighter than or something: or so hedges the quantity and nothing else, which is why it survives in careful writing.
examples: It's a mile or so from here.
Give it twenty minutes or so and check it again.
There were thirty people or so in the room.
She's been gone a week or so.
The whole repair came to four hundred dollars or so.
entries.русский: примерно / около того — после числа, времени или расстояния
entries.variants: or thereabouts, or so ago
entries.see also: -ish, more or less, or something, kind of

entries.meaning: Tacked onto an uncertain detail to mark it as approximate — you are giving the gist, not the fact. It also softens a suggestion into something the listener can easily turn down.
examples: He's a consultant or something — I've never really understood his job.
We could grab coffee or something this week.
It cost two hundred dollars or something like that.
She said she was going to Portland or something.
Did you leave it in the car or something?
entries.русский: или что-то в этом роде — помечает деталь как приблизительную
entries.variants: or something like that, or somethin'
entries.see also: or whatever, and stuff, kind of, I dunno

entries.meaning: Closes an option or a list with a shrug, signaling that the exact item does not matter to you. Depending on tone it is either easygoing or openly indifferent, so it is risky when the details matter to the person you are talking to.
examples: Bring chips, soda, or whatever — it's not a fancy party.
We can meet Tuesday, Wednesday, or whatever works for you.
He's studying economics or whatever — some business thing.
Just leave it on the porch or whatever.
She wanted the corner office, the title, or whatever it is people want.
entries.русский: или что там ещё / или как его — закрывает список пожатием плеч; может звучать безразлично
entries.variants: or whatever it is, or whatever you call it
entries.see also: or something, and stuff, and whatnot, blah blah blah

entries.meaning: Means "almost entirely," and works as a hedge that keeps a strong statement from being an absolute one. Americans use it constantly, often where a British speaker would reach for more or less.
examples: That's pretty much everything I know about it.
The season is pretty much over at this point.
"Are you packed?" "Pretty much."
He pretty much admitted he'd forgotten the whole thing.
We eat the same dinner pretty much every night.
entries.pronunciation note: the t is a quick flap, like the d in ladder
entries.русский: почти что / практически — «почти полностью», разг.
entries.variants: just about, pretty much it
entries.see also: more or less, basically, kind of, -ish

entries.meaning: Flags the words just used as figurative, borrowed, or not quite the right ones, so the listener does not take them at face value. It is the exact opposite of literally, and it is comfortable in writing as well as speech.
examples: He jumped ship, so to speak, about a month before the merger.
We're flying blind, so to speak, until the survey comes back.
She's the mayor of that whole neighborhood, so to speak.
The account has been in a coma, so to speak, since March.
I'm the referee, so to speak, whenever those two get going.
entries.русский: так сказать / если можно так выразиться — слова употреблены фигурально
entries.variants: as it were, in a manner of speaking
entries.see also: literally, kind of, more or less, if that makes sense

entries.meaning: The near-twin of kind of: it hedges a description down to "partly" or "in a way." The difference is slight — sort of feels marginally more bookish, kind of more all-purpose — and either one can hedge a single word or a whole sentence.
examples: I sort of knew this was coming.
It's sorta like tennis, but on a smaller court.
"Are you two dating?" "Sort of. It's complicated."
The whole trip was sort of a disaster.
He sort of apologized, if you can call it that.
entries.русский: вроде / как бы / отчасти — почти то же, что kind of, чуть книжнее
entries.variants: sorta, sort of like
entries.see also: kind of, -ish, I guess, like

entries.meaning: Marks a statement as true by the strict letter of the rule while hinting that the spirit of the rule points somewhere else. It hedges and corrects at the same time, and aimed at someone else's sentence it is a small act of pedantry that Americans find funny and irritating in about equal measure.
examples: Technically, the store closed five minutes ago.
She's technically my stepsister, but we grew up in the same house.
"You're late." "Technically I'm on time — the meeting starts at ten after."
Technically speaking, none of this is in my job description.
It's technically legal, which is not the same thing as a good idea.
entries.русский: формально / строго говоря — по букве верно, хотя по сути не совсем
entries.register: neutral (as a lone objection it sounds pedantic)
entries.variants: technically speaking, well, technically, technically, yes
entries.see also: actually, literally, kind of, well

entries.meaning: Introduces the point that cuts against what you have just said, usually in defense of somebody who is not in the room. It advertises that you are being even-handed on purpose — and used constantly, especially online, it starts to read as reflexive contrarianism.
examples: To be fair, nobody told him the deadline had moved.
The food took forever, but to be fair, they were packed.
In fairness, she did offer to pay for half.
"He never proofreads anything." "To be fair, neither do you."
I complained the entire drive — to be fair, it was six hours.
entries.русский: справедливости ради / надо отдать должное — довод против только что сказанного
entries.variants: in fairness, to be fair to him, TBF, tbf
entries.see also: to be honest, granted, that said, I mean

entries.meaning: Braces the listener for a blunt or unflattering opinion and asks in advance to be forgiven for it. It does not really claim that everything before it was dishonest, though a listener who wants to take it that way can.
examples: To be honest, I'd rather not go.
The first album was better, to be honest.
To be perfectly honest, I forgot you were coming.
"What did you think?" "Honestly? It needs work."
TBH I never finished the book.
entries.русский: честно говоря / если честно — сейчас будет резкое или нелестное мнение
entries.register: informal (the abbreviation TBH is for texting only)
entries.variants: honestly, to be perfectly honest, if I'm being honest, TBH, tbh
entries.see also: to be fair, I mean, I feel like, look, well

entries.meaning: Invites the listener to fill in the rest, either because the point is obvious or because you would rather not spell it out. In heavy use it becomes a pure filler that shows up every few words, and that is the version people get criticized for.
examples: It's just been one of those weeks, you know?
He's, y'know, not exactly a people person.
You know, I was thinking the exact same thing.
She wants to travel more while she still can, you know?
It's not that I'm mad, it's just — you know.
Know what I mean? Nobody wants to be the one to bring it up.
entries.русский: понимаешь / знаешь — приглашает додумать остальное; в избытке — чистый филлер
entries.variants: y'know, ya know, know what I mean, you know what I'm saying
entries.see also: I mean, like, see, you see, and stuff

entries.meaning: Stands in for talk the speaker considers predictable, tedious, or not worth repeating. It dismisses the content rather than the listener — unless you use it while someone is still talking.
examples: The email was all "we value your feedback," blah blah blah.
He gave the usual speech about teamwork, blah blah blah.
Terms and conditions, privacy policy, blah blah blah — just click accept.
She started in on how busy she's been, blah blah blah.
Blah blah blah — get to the part where somebody fixes it.
entries.русский: бла-бла-бла — вместо предсказуемой, скучной болтовни
entries.variants: blah blah, blah-blah-blah
entries.see also: yada yada, or whatever, and stuff

entries.meaning: A placeholder for a small gadget or part whose name you do not know, typically something mechanical or electronic that you can point at. It sounds homey and a little old-fashioned.
examples: Hand me that doohickey with the red button on it.
There's a little doohickey on the back that adjusts the height.
"What's this thing for?" "That doohickey keeps the door from slamming."
I lost the doohickey that came with the blender.
You need some kind of doohickey to open the battery compartment.
entries.русский: штуковина / фиговина — разг., мелкая деталька или приспособление без названия
entries.variants: doohicky, dohickey, doodad
entries.see also: gizmo, thingamajig, thingy, whatsit, whatchamacallit

entries.meaning: A placeholder for a gadget, usually an electronic one, carrying a hint that the speaker thinks it is clever, unnecessary, or both. Where doohickey sounds folksy and mechanical, gizmo sounds modern and slightly skeptical.
examples: His car is full of gizmos he has never once used.
There's a gizmo on the dashboard that tells you the tire pressure.
She bought some gizmo that's supposed to sharpen knives.
"What's that?" "Some gizmo my brother sent me for my birthday."
The kitchen drawer is nothing but gizmos and dead batteries.
entries.русский: гаджет / хитрая штуковина — разг. об электронной приблуде, часто с иронией
entries.variants: gismo, gizmos
entries.see also: doohickey, thingamajig, thingy, whatsit

entries.meaning: A stand-in for a person whose name does not matter or is not being supplied — useful when you are describing a pattern rather than a case. Keep the separate insult sense in mind: that old so-and-so is a polite substitute for a much stronger word, and it is affectionate about as often as it is not.
examples: They'll announce that so-and-so is retiring and everyone will act surprised.
You can't tell the client that so-and-so dropped the ball and leave it there.
Every single year so-and-so forgets to book the room.
"Who signs off on it?" "So-and-so in legal — I'd have to look up the name."
He called me a stubborn old so-and-so and then bought me a beer.
entries.русский: такой-то — вместо неназванного человека; как мягкая брань — «такой-сякой» (эвфемизм)
entries.register: informal (as an insult it is a euphemism — mild on the page, but it stands in for a much stronger word)
entries.variants: Mr. So-and-so, so and so, such-and-such a person
entries.see also: whatshisname, such and such, thingy, whatchamacallit

entries.meaning: A stand-in for an unspecified detail — a date, an amount, a name — used when you are sketching how something generally goes rather than reporting a particular case. It almost always turns up inside a hypothetical.
examples: The letter says you owe such and such an amount by such and such a date.
They want a form saying you worked at such-and-such a company for five years.
You call, you sit on hold, and they tell you to press such and such a number.
He'll swear the meeting was on such-and-such a day and nobody can prove otherwise.
"Just fill in the blanks — name, address, such and such."
entries.русский: такой-то / такое-то — вместо неуказанной даты, суммы или названия
entries.variants: such-and-such, such and such a thing
entries.see also: so-and-so, whatchamacallit, and whatnot, yada yada

entries.meaning: A nonsense elaboration of thing, used for an object whose name has escaped you at that moment. It is longer and more playful than thingy, and it almost always comes with a gesture.
examples: Where's that thingamajig for opening wine bottles?
He's got a thingamajig on his keychain that measures the temperature.
Push the little thingamabob on the side to reset it.
The thingamajig under the sink started leaking again.
I need one of those thingamajigs that keeps the cord from tangling.
entries.русский: штуковина / загогулина — шутливое разрастание слова «штука»
entries.variants: thingamabob, thingumajig, thingummy
entries.see also: doohickey, thingy, whatchamacallit, whatsit

entries.meaning: The shortest and most common placeholder noun, used for an object — and sometimes for a person, an event, or a quirk — when the real word will not come. Very frequent in casual speech and easy to overuse.
examples: Can you pass me that thingy on the counter?
There's a thingy in the app that shows how much data you've used.
She has a thingy about people wearing shoes in the house.
The plastic thingy on my charger broke off.
We're doing the thingy at Dave's on Saturday, right?
entries.русский: штука / штучка — самый короткий и частый заменитель забытого слова
entries.variants: thingie
entries.see also: thingamajig, whatchamacallit, whatsit, doohickey

entries.meaning: A compressed "what you may call it," dropped into a sentence in place of an object or a place whose name you have lost. Saying it usually invites the listener to supply the missing word.
examples: Grab the — whatchamacallit — the spatula, the wide one.
He works at that whatchamacallit downtown, the co-working place.
I need a whatchamacallit to get the lid off.
She used the whatchacallit, the paddle attachment.
It's right next to the whaddayacallit, the old post office.
entries.русский: как эта штука называется / как его там — вместо забытого названия предмета
entries.variants: whatchacallit, whaddayacallit, whatchamacallem
entries.see also: whatsit, thingy, thingamajig, what's the word

entries.meaning: A placeholder for a person whose name you cannot recall or cannot be bothered to use. The -face versions are blunter and usually carry a little contempt.
examples: Whatshisname from accounting stopped by looking for you.
Wasn't she married to whatshisname, the guy with the boat?
I ran into whatshername from your old office at the airport.
What's-his-face still hasn't returned my email.
It was directed by whatshisname — he did that space movie.
entries.русский: как его там / как бишь его зовут — вместо имени человека; пренебрежительно
entries.register: informal (dismissive about the person named — not something to say to their face; the -face forms are ruder still)
entries.variants: whatshername, whatsisname, what's-his-face, what's-her-face
entries.see also: whatchamacallit, so-and-so, thingy, what's the word

entries.meaning: A short placeholder built out of "what is it," used for a small object or, in the -name form, for a thing or person whose name is gone. Americans understand it and use it occasionally, but it is a British habit at heart, and in an American mouth it can sound slightly put on.
examples: Hand me the whatsit, the little metal clip.
It's in the whatsit — the drawer next to the fridge.
He fixed it with a screwdriver and some kind of rubber whatsit.
We stayed at the whatsitsname, the place with the red awning.
There's a whatsit missing from the box.
entries.русский: штуковина / как его — брит., из «what is it»; американец скорее скажет thingy
entries.register: informal (chiefly British; an American is far likelier to reach for thingy or whatchamacallit)
entries.variants: whatsits, whatsis, whatsitsname
entries.see also: whatchamacallit, doohickey, thingy

entries.meaning: Skips over a stretch of a story that is boring, obvious, or awkward to spell out: "and so on, you can fill in the rest." Made famous nationally by a 1997 episode of Seinfeld, it now often implies that the speaker is glossing over the interesting part on purpose.
examples: We argued, we made up, yada yada, now we're married.
He gave me the whole speech about responsibility, yada yada yada.
So I go in, fill out the forms, yada yada, and they still say I'm not in the system.
Dinner, drinks, yada yada — it was a long night.
She said she was sorry, yada yada, but nothing actually changed.
entries.русский: и так далее / бла-бла — пропуск скучной или неловкой части истории
entries.variants: yada yada yada, yadda yadda, yaddayadda
entries.see also: blah blah blah, and stuff, or whatever
